children: By Paul Vieira

OTTAWA--The Trump administration's taunting of Canada isn't constructive and should cease if the U.S. is serious about clinching a beneficial trade deal with its northern neighbor, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said.

"When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions," Carney said to reporters Tuesday in Ottawa.
"But, look, it's not constructive. That's their democracy," he added.

The prime minister's remarks were a rebuttal to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blaming the Canadian leader for the collapse of trade talks last month. Bessent also brushed off concerns about igniting a trade war with the U.S.'s second-largest trading partner, after Mexico, by noting that the American economy dwarfs Canada's.

Bessent also joked that Canada might send mini-submarines previously used on an amusement-park ride to attack the U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, on the X social-media platform, published a post showing two female Canadian cadets which was interpreted as mocking the cadets' weight and gender.
"It's beneath their office," Carney said of the Trump administration's mocking of Canada's armed forces.

The Trump administration has ramped up its attacks following the breakdown of talks that could have sharply reduced tariffs from hefty levels on key Canadian goods such as steel, aluminum and motor vehicles.

The U.S. and Canadian sides blame each other for the collapse, arguing their counterpart introduced last-minute demands that made an agreement untenable. Carney said Tuesday the two sides were moving toward a mutually beneficial deal, but it was never finalized and interests separated at the end.
"At some point, maybe it'll converge again," he added.

White House spokesman Kush Desai said that, among U.S. trading partners, Canada was offered the most generous trade deal. Instead, Canada rejected the proposal, and made further demands and offered little in return, he added.

"President Trump was given a resounding Election Day mandate to put American workers, farmers, and businesses first, and the administration will continue to deliver while lowering costs for everyday families," Desai said.

Following the disintegration of trade talks last month, the U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian imports. Canada intends to retaliate with a tariff package of its own, with duties ranging from 15% to 50% on about $20 billion of U.S. goods, effective next Tuesday.

President Trump ramped up the stakes by threatening a 50% tariff on all Canadian-assembled motor vehicles and automotive parts starting on Jan. 1, 2027--a move that threatens to upend the closely integrated North American auto sector.

Trump also angered the Canadian public when he ordered that one of the Great Lakes, Lake Ontario, be renamed Lake America, after the premier of Ontario called Trump a "dictator," "loser," and "king of bankruptcies." Google said it incorporated the name change for U.S. users of its maps app.

Polling indicates the Carney government enjoys solid public support for his U.S. trade strategy, and the prime minister said that helped his Liberal Party collect victories in three special elections on Monday night, including picking up a district in Quebec previously held by the Conservative Party.

Carney said Canada walked away from the negotiating table because of, among other things, U.S. efforts to treat core Canadian industries like U.S. subsidiaries, setting the stage for those sectors to "be gradually wound down in Canada and wiped out."

He added that the U.S. also made demands that would closely align Canada's trade policy with Washington's, thereby threatening Ottawa's capacity to strike new commercial trade agreements with India, and economies in southeast Asia and South America.
"Of course, we are not going to accept those terms," the prime minister said.
